name: Self-Interruption
summary: Breaking off your own task with no external trigger (e.g., to check email or jump to another task), which happens about as often as being interrupted by others.
explanation:
A self-interruption is a switch away from your current task that nobody else caused. No notification, colleague or call triggered it: you just stop and go check something.

Field studies by Gloria Mark and colleagues found that knowledge workers interrupt themselves about as often as other people interrupt them. Jing Jin and Laura Dabbish (2009) sorted self-interruptions by cause: adjusting the work environment, taking a break, checking for updates, following an inquiry that the task raised, recalling something else that needs doing, waiting, and plain routine. Many of these are habits that the attention economy trained into us. Some are an escape from a task that feels hard or boring.

Self-interruptions cost just as much as external ones. Each one leaves attention residue and adds a resumption lag. It also makes it less likely that you finish the original task in one session. And since the trigger is internal, blocking notifications alone won't fix it.

So how do you reduce them? Write a stray thought or task down instead of acting on it (a capture habit or an interstitial journal helps here). Schedule shallow work like email in fixed slots, so the urge has a known outlet. Work in timed focus blocks. And notice when the urge to switch is really telling you that the current task is unclear or too big.
